title: What goes into our post-tour follow-up

content.job: Standalone list email. Tell the full exchange from more tours and unanswered follow-up to the client's within-a-week practice and prospective texts. Connect the point to the complete LeadLock system with one reply invitation.
content.body:
She told me she pays attention to one thing during a tour: whether her venue is the first stop on the couple's list or the final one.

When she knows she was the final stop, she follows up within the week and puts the question plainly but kindly. Have they chosen a venue, or are they still undecided? It's a fair question for a couple who has finished looking, and their answer helps her know how to proceed.

A couple fresh off their first tour is somewhere else entirely. They're still comparing, and asking them to decide would come too early.

**A tour tells you a couple came to visit, but what you learn during it tells you how close they are to choosing.**

She already had automated follow-up emails in place, and she was reaching out personally on top of them. She'd been wondering about adding texts after the tour as well, and I agreed we could incorporate them.

What stayed with me from that conversation is how much good follow-up depends on something the venue already knows. You're the one walking couples through the space. You hear whether they have other visits coming up or whether yours was the last one they planned. When we shape the emails and texts that go out after a tour, that's the knowledge we want them to rest on, so a couple who's still comparing and a couple who's ready to decide each hear something that fits.

LeadLock is the platform where we build your email and text follow-up. That includes The Foolproof Follow-Up Advantage, our email-and-text follow-up system, set up around your own conversations with couples. You run the platform, and the personal contact couples get from you stays in your hands.
content.ending:
If you'd like follow-up support shaped around what you learn on your tours, simply reply to this email and let's talk about your business.

Talk soon,
Whitney

content.title: First tour or last tour (client call)
content.script:
I had a call with one of our venue clients recently, and she was booking more tours, but more of those couples were going quiet afterwards.

So I asked her a question. When couples leave a tour, do they still have other venues to see, or are they ready to move forward?

And she explained that she gauges one thing: is her venue their first tour, or their last?

When she knows it's their last, she reaches out within a week and asks, really politely, if they've made their choice or they're still undecided.

I thought that was such a smart distinction.

Because a couple who's just started touring is still comparing, right? They're not necessarily ready for that question yet.

Now, she already had automated emails going out, and she was following up personally on top of that. She'd been thinking about texting couples after the tour, too, and I told her we could add that.

So when we shape follow-up after a tour, the fact that a couple visited is only part of the picture. We want to know what they're ready to do next, so every email and text supports the conversation you're already having with them.

caption.body:
You walked them through the property, heard their questions and watched them picture the day. Then the follow-up has to meet each of them where they are, whether this was the first venue they've seen or the last one they planned to visit.

That's what I was asking about on a recent call with one of our venue clients. I wanted to know whether couples left with more visits ahead of them or ready to move forward.

Her answer was a distinction she pays attention to: first stop or final stop. After a final stop, she gets in touch within a week and asks, kindly and plainly, whether they've made a decision or are still undecided. A couple at the start of their search doesn't need that question yet.

She was already pairing automated emails with her own personal outreach, and when she raised adding post-tour texts, I agreed we could incorporate them.

That's the part of follow-up we care about most. The emails and texts should lean on what you've learned in person, so the next message fits the point the couple has actually reached.
caption.hook: You know things about a couple after a tour that no inbox can tell you.

So I asked what couples were ready to do when they left. Did they still have other venues to see, or were they ready to move forward?

She explained that she gauges whether her venue is their first tour or their last.

And when she knows it's their last, she follows up directly, within a week. Very politely, she asks whether they've chosen a venue or they're still undecided.

A couple who's just started touring is still comparing venues. They're not necessarily ready for that same question.

She already had automated emails, and she was following up personally, too. She brought up adding texts after the tour, and I agreed that we could incorporate them.

When we're thinking about the follow-up, we need more than the fact that a couple visited. We want to know what they're ready to do, so the messages can support the conversation you're having with them.

Your conversations on the tour can tell us what the next message needs to make room for, while email and text support the contact you continue to have with the couple.

content.job: Shows a venue owner how the weeks between a couple booking a tour and arriving for it can carry a personal next step, through one client's practice and Whitney's suggestion.
beats: Open on the gap between booking a tour more than two weeks out and the tour itself.

content.title: Tours booked weeks out
content.script:
When a couple books a venue tour more than two weeks out, what happens in those weeks in between?

I was on a call with one of our venue clients, and she told me that's the booking she wants to bring in sooner, because the couple might find something else before they ever get to her. So whenever she spots one, she sends a message herself, offering earlier openings and letting them know the original date is no problem either.

Some couples can move it. Some can't, like one couple who needed to wait until the whole family could come.

And her venue doesn't do tours on Saturdays when there's a wedding. So I wondered out loud about using a virtual tour for those couples. Maybe a phone call first, with a little behind-the-scenes look so they know what to expect. Or, if she has the bandwidth, a quick ten-minute FaceTime on an actual wedding day, so they see everything set up, because their in-person tour won't be on a wedding day.

She liked that idea. And I told her I think she can definitely keep sending her message, and depending on how a couple responds, that could shape her next step, maybe a video.

That gap before the tour is part of the follow-up, too. It's a chance to give couples a reason to want to see your venue in person.

caption.body:
For a venue, a tour booked far out can feel like a long wait. The couple is still planning and still looking, and you won't see them in person until the date arrives.

One of our venue clients keeps an eye on exactly this. When a couple books more than two weeks ahead, she writes to them personally, offers earlier times and lets them know their original date works too. Some couples move it. Others can't, like one couple who needed the whole family there.

We talked through what else that stretch of time could hold. I suggested a phone call with a short virtual look behind the scenes, or, when the day allows, a quick FaceTime during a wedding so the couple sees the space fully set up. Her venue doesn't give tours on wedding Saturdays, so that's a view they wouldn't otherwise get before visiting.

She liked the idea. Her first message would still go out, and the couple's reply would help decide which step makes sense next.

The time before a tour is part of your conversation with a couple, and a personal touch there gives them a reason to keep your venue on their list.

content.title: Welcome video by text

caption.body:
A couple who inquires is still deciding which venues are worth a visit, and your first reply is part of that decision.

I talked this through with a venue client we work with, starting from what her very first reply could hold. I suggested a short video with her on camera, introducing herself and the venue, then cutting to wedding footage or giving a quick behind-the-scenes look. She pictured it as the first text a couple receives after inquiring: a personal welcome from her with a quick virtual tour.

Why text? Inboxes get chaotic, and I said people are more likely to see or answer a text than an email. She felt that was very true for her couples. The video could live on YouTube, with the link in the message, and I think it could go to every couple who inquires, not only those booking tours far ahead.

This was an idea we talked through together. What we want a video like that to do is leave a couple feeling they should see the venue for themselves before they commit anywhere else.
